transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; what brings you in to see me today?

Well, Dr. Smith, it's nice to meet you too, though I wish it were under different circumstances, if you know what I mean. I’m here because my wife finally put her foot down, and honestly, I can’t say she’s entirely wrong. It’s this forgetfulness. It’s getting to be a real problem, a real nuisance. I keep forgetting things I really shouldn’t be forgetting at my age, you know? Important things. Like, just last month, I completely missed a heart follow-up appointment. Dr. Miller's office called, and I swear I meant to call them back to reschedule, but it just completely slipped my mind. Gone. Poof. And it’s not just the doctors, though that’s bad enough. I’ll go over to my buddy Al’s house—he lives just down the street, we’ve known each other for thirty years—I’ll head over there to help him fix his porch railing or something, and I’ll get all the way there and realize I left the drill, or the specific screws we talked about, sitting right on my workbench in the garage. It’s frustrating, you know? I’m 68, I’m retired, I should have the time to get these things right, but my brain just feels like a sieve lately. I’m always moving, always doing something, but I just can't seem to hold onto the important details when I need them.
Over what period of time have you noticed these memory issues becoming more frequent?

Well, let me think back... it’s been, gosh, I’d say it’s been causing real, noticeable trouble for about a year and two months now. I remember the timeline pretty clearly because it all started getting really bad right after my cardiac scare. You see, before that happened, I was always on the go. I’d be out walking the neighborhood for miles, tinkering in the garage for hours on end, building birdhouses, fixing lawnmowers, just keeping my hands and my feet busy. It kept me settled, you know? It burned off all that extra energy I've always had. But then I had the heart issue, and the doctors—Dr. Miller and the rest of them—they told me I had to take it easy. They said, "Slow down, Arthur, you can't be pushing yourself like you used to." So, I had to cut way back on the walking. I couldn't be lifting heavy things in the garage anymore. And sitting still... well, sitting still has never been my strong suit. I’m always tapping my foot or needing to get up and pace. So, without all those projects and the long walks to burn it off, I feel like my brain just started spinning its wheels. It’s like, because my body isn't moving as much, my mind is moving twice as fast, and all the important things—like appointments or where I put my keys or the drill for Al's porch—they just fly right out the window. So yeah, about fourteen months of this really frustrating forgetfulness, right since I had to slow down.
Aside from the memory lapses, have you noticed any changes in your ability to manage your daily finances, follow complex recipes, or find the right words when you are speaking?

Finances? Oh, no, no problems there. I mean, Mary—my wife—she handles the big household bills, the utilities and all that, she’s always done that because she likes the routine of it, sitting down on Sunday mornings with her tea. But I still manage my own accounts, you know, my little retirement fund for my projects and tools. Just the other day I went down to the hardware store to pick up some lumber—well, I couldn't carry much because of what the doctors said about my heart, but I bought some smaller pieces for a new birdhouse I'm trying to put together—and I knew exactly what I had in the account. I balanced the checkbook right there at the counter. The cashier, young kid, looked at me like I was an alien for using a paper checkbook, but my math is as sharp as it ever was. So the money is fine, no confusion there at all. 

And recipes... well, to be honest, Doc, I don't really cook complex things. Never have. Mary is a saint in the kitchen, she handles all that. Now, I do grill! I'm the grill master in the family. I make this barbecue chicken, marinate it overnight in this special sauce—it's just ketchup, brown sugar, a little apple cider vinegar, and a dash of cayenne, but don't tell anyone my secret—and I never forget how to do that. I know all the steps by heart. Though, I will admit, standing by the grill waiting for the chicken to cook drives me absolutely up the wall. I have to be flipping it, moving it around, scraping the grates, or pacing around the patio because I just can't stand just standing there watching it cook. But no, I don't get confused by the steps or anything like that. 

And as for finding words? Ha! If anything, Mary would tell you I have way too many words. I can talk the ear off a brass monkey. I was just talking to Al the other day—the guy with the porch I mentioned earlier—and we stood out there for an hour just shooting the breeze about the neighborhood association and the new stop sign they put in down on 4th street. I never lose my train of thought when I'm talking, I don't forget what things are called. I just... I just have a lot to say, I guess. Always have. So no, none of that stuff you mentioned is giving me any grief. It's really just the forgetting where I put things, or the appointments, like I was saying. My brain is fine with the words and the math, it just won't hold onto the schedule!

Arthur, you mentioned that you feel like your mind is spinning its wheels, but do you find that you spend a significant amount of your day feeling uncontrollably worried or anxious about a wide variety of different topics, such as your health, your finances, or your family's safety?

Worried? Anxious? Oh, no, no, no, Doc, that’s not it at all. I mean, sure, the heart thing gave me a bit of a jolt—anyone would be a little spooked when they tell you your ticker’s acting up, right? But I’m not sitting around wringing my hands about it. I take my pills, I do what Dr. Miller says—well, when I remember to go to the appointments, anyway! But no, I’m not losing sleep thinking I’m going to drop dead tomorrow. And Mary and the kids—they’re all grown, doing fine. Jimmy’s got a great job over at the plant, and Sarah just had her second baby, little girl, cute as a button. I don’t worry about them, they’ve got good heads on their shoulders. 

And like I said about the money, we’re comfortable. We’re not rich, we’re not taking cruises to the Bahamas every winter like some folks, but the house is paid off, and my pension covers what we need. So I’m not stewing over the bills, either. 

When I say my mind is spinning its wheels, it’s not worry. It’s more like... like a motor that’s running too fast, you know? Like when you’ve got a car in neutral and you just keep revving the engine. It’s not going anywhere, but it’s making a lot of noise and burning up gas. That’s what it feels like up here. I’m just restless. I’ll be sitting in my recliner, trying to watch the evening news with Mary—she likes the local broadcast, likes to see what the weather’s going to do—and I just can’t stay put. My foot starts tapping, my fingers start drumming on the armrest. I’ll think, "Oh, I should go check if I closed the garage door," or "I wonder if I have enough of those 1-inch nails for the birdhouse." And before I know it, I’m up and pacing around the living room, and Mary’s telling me to sit down because I’m blocking the TV. 

It’s just this energy, Doc. This constant need to be doing something, fixing something, moving something. And since I can’t do all the heavy lifting and the long walks like I used to, all that energy just gets bottled up and bounces around in my head, knocking all the important thoughts—like the appointments and the drill for Al’s porch—right out of place. But it’s not worry. I’m not an anxious guy. I’m just a guy who can’t seem to sit still, even when he really needs to.

Arthur, looking back at your younger years, even when you were very active, did you find that you were often described as restless, easily distracted, or someone who had trouble staying focused on one task for a long time?

Ha! Well, if you asked my mother—God rest her soul—she’d probably laugh right out loud at that one. You hit the nail right on the head, Doc. It’s not just a recent thing, no sir. Even way back when I was just a little boy in grade school, I was exactly the same way. I was always the kid who just absolutely could not stay in his seat. They had those old wooden desks back then, you know, the heavy ones with the cast iron sides that were practically bolted to the floor, and I’d still be squirming out of mine. I'd be leaning over to see what the kid next to me was drawing, or getting up to sharpen my pencil for the fifth time before lunch. I just couldn't stay put.

And focus? Well, if the teacher was talking, my brain was already three steps ahead, or out the window watching the janitor rake the leaves. I remember my third-grade teacher, Mrs. Gable—strict woman, wore these thick glasses and always had her hair pulled back real tight—she’d ask the class a question about history or spelling, and I wouldn't even think to raise my hand. I’d just blurt the answer right out before she even finished the sentence! I just couldn't hold it in. The thought would pop into my head and shoot right out of my mouth before anyone else even had a chance to blink. 

I can't tell you how many times I got notes sent home for talking too much. It was a regular occurrence, practically a weekly tradition. I’d come home, and my mother would find this little slip of paper pinned to my coat or folded up in my reading book saying, "Arthur is a bright boy, but he disrupts the class," or "Arthur talks when he should be listening." I just always had a lot of energy and a lot to say, and I couldn't just sit quietly and stare at a chalkboard for hours on end. 

So, yeah, looking back, that restlessness, that jumping from one thing to another... that’s just always been Arthur. It worked out fine for most of my life because I found ways to stay busy, out building things and moving around all day, working with my hands. But now that the doctors have me stuck in the recliner resting my heart... well, like I said, the engine is still running just as hot as it did in Mrs. Gable's class! I just don't have anywhere to drive the car anymore.
